Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Retired
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 66

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Busyness: I work hard at keeping busy with other things, Avoid People: avoid other people, Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
  Threat: Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
  Negative Appraisals: Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
Mary, a 68-year-old North American woman, has been struggling with the aftermath of her husband’s unexpected death. Mary had always considered herself strong-warm-hearted yet resilient—but after losing her partner of over four decades to a sudden heart attack, she found herself in uncharted emotional territory. The day her world changed was one that started like any other: sunny and peaceful. Her husband, John, had left for his morning walk at the park as usual. Mary stayed behind to finish up some light housework, preparing for their plans to visit friends later that afternoon. She received a call from the hospital—John had collapsed and died on the spot. The news hit her like a freight train; she felt the ground beneath her give way. In the weeks following John’s death, Mary found herself working hard at keeping busy with other things to avoid dwelling on her loss. She immersed herself in household chores and routine activities, often staying up late into the night. Her efforts to keep her mind occupied led her to neglect much-needed rest and self-care. This busyness became a coping mechanism, but it also isolated her from any meaningful connection. Mary’s social life suffered as she began avoiding people altogether, especially those with whom she used to socialize frequently. She found it increasingly difficult to engage in conversations that reminded her of John or the life they once shared together. Simple outings like grocery shopping became overwhelming; the sight of a familiar face could trigger intense emotions and feelings of isolation. Her body remained on high alert at all times, tense and ready to react to any perceived danger. Even when she was aware of being in safe environments, Mary’s muscles would tighten, her heart rate would elevate, and her mind raced with anxious thoughts. She struggled to relax even while sitting quietly at home, surrounded by memories that now felt like a stark reminder of her loss. Mary had come to believe that she should have protected John from his sudden death, but the reality was that there were no warning signs or preventative measures she could have taken. This sense of failure gnawed at her, adding layers of guilt and shame to her already heavy emotional burden. She felt isolated and set apart from others, as if no one truly understood what she had experienced or how it changed her. Her marriage and the life they built together were now tinged with regret and an overwhelming sense that she didn’t belong anywhere without John by her side. Mary’s social contacts dwindled further, and even close friends found themselves at a loss on how to support her effectively. Her children noticed the changes but felt helpless in their efforts to reach out. The cumulative effect of these behaviors began to show in various aspects of her daily life. Mary grew increasingly isolated from her community and lost touch with people she once considered dear friends. This disconnection made it harder for her to cope with the daily reminders of John’s absence, leaving her feeling more alone than ever. What frightened her most was the thought that this void would never be filled and that she was destined to live in a constant state of fear and isolation. Despite her efforts to keep busy and avoid painful memories, Mary realized that she needed help to navigate through these emotions. The overwhelming sense of failure and guilt finally pushed her to seek professional support. In therapy, Mary is most hoping for a way to find some solace and healing. She dreams of feeling less isolated and more connected with others, but also acknowledges the fear that opening up might bring back painful memories she’s been trying so hard to avoid. Despite these fears, Mary remains determined to work through her grief and rediscover parts of herself that have felt lost since John's passing.
